name: Kayako
tagline: A 2001-vintage helpdesk relaunched under private-equity ownership as a pay-per-resolution AI agent, with the seat-based product it used to be quietly folded underneath.
tldr: Kayako is a long-running omnichannel helpdesk (email, live chat, social, plus a claimed voice channel) that has been repositioned around 'Kay', an AI agent that triages, drafts, takes actions like refunds, and closes tickets autonomously.

Pricing is the headline change: kayako.com/pricing now advertises '$1 Per Resolved Ticket' with 'no seat fees' and no setup fees, though multiple third-party trackers still describe a roughly $79/month Kayako One base alongside it — the two accounts contradict each other and Kayako does not publish enough detail to settle it.

Founded in 2001 by Varun Shoor and Jamie Edwards, bootstrapped with no external funding, and acquired by ESW Capital in February 2018 — the Joe Liemandt private-equity group that has rolled up roughly 75 mature software companies and staffs them through its Crossover contractor platform.

Capterra shows 4.0/5 across 176 reviews and Trustpilot 4.3/5 across just 22, with the AI agent drawing genuine recent praise; reviewers in the same breath call analytics 'the weak spot' and say there are no good voice options.

The real weakness is verifiability: the 68% AI resolution rate is a vendor claim with no independent audit, and the flagship case studies on the homepage are Trilogy and Aurea — sister companies under the same owner, not arm's-length customers.

Best for small-to-mid support teams whose ticket mix is genuinely repetitive and who want to pay for outcomes rather than seats — provided they can tolerate an opaque price and a product whose long-term roadmap is not publicly committed.
keyFeatures: Kay AI agent that reads tickets, drafts replies, triages, and resolves cases end-to-end — billed only when it closes an issue without human escalation
Agentic actions beyond replying: Kay can create users, issue refunds, update records, and close tickets rather than only writing text
Automatic knowledge base article drafting when a ticket escalates to a human, with an approve-or-edit step before publishing
SingleView customer context pulling a contact's history across channels into one view
Omnichannel inbox covering email, live chat, and social in a single ticket queue
Knowledge base with semantic search powering both self-service and Kay's answers
No-code workflow automation rules plus SLA management and reporting dashboards
Enterprise security posture: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, and SSO/SAML per Kayako's own site
Prebuilt connections to Slack, Stripe, Shopify, Salesforce, HubSpot, Twilio, Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom, and custom APIs

companyInfo.hq: London, United Kingdom (originally founded in Jalandhar, India); current operations run under ESW Capital, based in Austin, Texas
companyInfo.funding: Bootstrapped with no external investment; acquired by ESW Capital on 14 February 2018 (deal value undisclosed)
companyInfo.employees: Not disclosed. Kayako publishes no headcount, and ESW Capital portfolio products are typically staffed through its Crossover remote-contractor platform rather than conventional employment — treat any employee figure you see elsewhere as unverified.

faq.question: Who owns Kayako now?
faq.answer: ESW Capital, the Austin-based private equity group controlled by Trilogy founder Joe Liemandt, acquired Kayako on 14 February 2018. ESW has acquired roughly 75 software companies and staffs acquired products through its affiliated Crossover contractor platform. Kayako was bootstrapped and had taken no external investment before the sale.

faq.question: What does Kayako actually cost?
faq.answer: This is genuinely unclear, and that matters. Kayako's own pricing page advertises '$1 Per Resolved Ticket' with 'no seat fees' and 'no setup fees', charging only when Kay fully resolves an issue without human escalation. But several third-party pricing trackers describe a Kayako One base of around $79/month sitting underneath that per-resolution charge. Kayako does not publish plan tables, billing terms, or contract minimums to settle the contradiction, and pricing runs through a sales conversation rather than a checkout. Assume you will need a quote.

faq.question: Is the 68% AI resolution rate real?
faq.answer: It is Kayako's own published figure and there is no independent audit of it. Kayako's homepage separately cites a 52% AI-resolved rate in a sample deployment, so even the vendor's own numbers span a wide range. Worth knowing: the flagship case studies behind those claims — Trilogy and Aurea — are ESW Capital sister companies under the same ownership, not independent customers, which makes them weak evidence for what a typical buyer should expect.

faq.question: Does Kayako support phone or voice support?
faq.answer: Kayako's homepage lists voice among its channels, but a Capterra reviewer in April 2026 stated plainly that 'they don't really have any great options for voice.' There is no detailed public voice documentation comparable to Zendesk Talk. If phone support is a core requirement, verify this in a demo before signing anything.

faq.question: How does Kayako's per-resolution price compare to competitors?
faq.answer: At $1 per resolution it is the most expensive per-resolution rate among the AI agents reviewed on this site — Intercom's Fin is $0.99 and Help Scout's AI Answers is $0.75. All three bill only on resolutions that close without human escalation. Intercom also sells Fin standalone at $0.99/resolution with no seats at all, layered onto a helpdesk you already own, which is a direct competitor to Kayako's 'no seat fees' pitch.

faq.question: Is Kayako still actively developed?
faq.answer: There is real evidence of recent product work — Kay is new, and Capterra reviews from April 2026 describe the AI agent as a current, functioning feature rather than vaporware. What is missing is any public roadmap, changelog, or release-notes feed, and ESW Capital's acquisition model is widely reported as buying mature software and running it lean. Recent reviews are also thin: only a handful postdate the AI pivot.

criteriaScores.note: Kayako's site lists email, live chat, social, and voice, but voice is the shakiest claim on the page — a Capterra reviewer (Uba A., VP of Growth, April 2026) said flatly that 'they don't really have any great options for voice', and there is no public voice documentation. No evidence found of native WhatsApp, Instagram DM, or SMS as first-class channels.

Kayako's SingleView feature is explicitly built to pull a customer's history across channels into one view, and the product is sold as an omnichannel inbox rather than per-channel queues (kayako.com). Scored 4 rather than 5 because the channel list it unifies is narrower than Zendesk's.

Kay is a genuine agentic AI, not canned smart-replies — Kayako documents it reading tickets, drafting replies, triaging, taking actions, and closing cases autonomously, and the entire pricing model is built on resolutions it completes without human escalation (kayako.com/pricing).

Kayako publishes a 68% AI resolution rate on its pricing page and a 52% figure in a homepage case study — a wide spread within the vendor's own marketing, with no independent audit. The named case studies (Trilogy, Aurea) are ESW Capital sister companies, so they are not arm's-length evidence.

Kayako states Kay 'learns from your tickets rather than operating as a generic model' and is backed by a knowledge base with semantic search — historical-ticket plus knowledge-source training, not manual intent trees (kayako.com). Docked one point because the ingestion and retraining mechanics are not documented publicly.

Genuinely agentic rather than if/then: Kayako documents Kay creating users, issuing refunds, updating data, and closing cases, on top of no-code workflow automation rules and SLA management. Not scored 5 because there is no public documentation of step limits, branching, or flow-builder depth comparable to Zendesk's Action Builder.

An omnichannel inbox plus SingleView customer context is the core of the product, and reviewers describe the ticket interface as lightweight and easy to navigate. One recurring, specific complaint on G2 is the lack of native auto-refresh, which creates friction in busy queues.

Escalation is structurally central — Kayako only bills the $1 fee when Kay resolves without human escalation, and the product auto-drafts a knowledge base article at the moment a ticket hands off to a human (kayako.com/pricing). The mechanics of what context transfers on handoff are not publicly documented in detail.

Ticket notes are a documented, well-reviewed feature — a Capterra reviewer (Natale M., Senior Field Technician, May 2025) specifically praised 'the ability to add notes to tickets' for managing work between users. Assignment and routing are covered by the automation rules and SLA tooling.

Shopify is named directly on kayako.com/pricing as one of the systems Kay connects to, and Kay is documented as able to issue refunds — but Kayako publishes no app listing or integration documentation describing the depth of the Shopify connection, so this is a vendor name-drop rather than a verified feature set.

Salesforce and HubSpot are both named as Kay connections on kayako.com/pricing, and Salesforce also appears on the homepage integration list. No evidence found of a Pipedrive integration, and no public documentation of sync direction or field mapping depth.

Stripe and Shopify are both named as connected systems, and Kayako explicitly claims Kay can 'issue refunds' and 'update data' — that is action on live commerce data rather than only talking about it. Scored 4 not 5 because there is no public setup documentation confirming this works out of the box versus requiring custom API work.

Triage is a documented Kay function, and a Trustpilot reviewer (Dmitry, May 2026) described Kay recognising a situation it should not handle, pulling a human in, and handing over a full summary — which implies working escalation detection. But Kayako publishes no sentiment scoring model, urgency scale, or frustration-detection field comparable to Zendesk's Intelligent Triage, so the depth here is inferred rather than documented.

Well documented and genuinely broad on the interface side — Kayako supports 44 languages, with the Help Center interface translated into 30+, and Messenger automatically switching to the user's stored language preference (support.kayako.com articles 1154, 1287, 1289). Scored 3 rather than 5 because this is localization plus manually translated content, not automatic detection and on-the-fly AI translation of agent replies the way Zendesk does it.

Reporting, analytics, and SLA management exist, but this is the most consistently criticised part of the product: a Capterra reviewer (David M., Admin, April 2026) called 'Analytics is the weak spot', and multiple review roundups describe data buried under menus that are not laid out intuitively.

Kayako advertises '$1 Per Resolved Ticket' with 'no seat fees' and calls it 'transparent pricing', but publishes no plan table, billing terms, contract minimums, or overage rules, and several third-party trackers report a roughly $79/month base the official page never mentions. Billing complaints are also the dominant theme in negative Trustpilot reviews — one customer reported 'erroneous invoices' after a documented cancellation (Fabian, July 2025), another an unexpected three-year invoice. A pricing claim independent sources contradict is not transparent, whichever figure is right.

Macros are properly documented and go well beyond canned text — Kayako's help center states a macro can perform eight distinct actions including inserting reply text, adding notes, and updating conversation fields in one click (support.kayako.com/article/1153-automating-common-replies-and-updates-using-macros). Macros are also available in the Android mobile app.

Kayako maintains an official Zapier app with its own setup article in the Kayako help center (support.kayako.com/article/1169), connecting ticket creation, status updates, and customer notifications to Zapier's wider app catalogue. No evidence found of native Make.com or n8n connectors, which is why this is not a 5.

There is a genuine public developer portal at developer.kayako.com documenting a REST API, plus help-center articles covering incoming webhooks for pushing external events onto Kayako timelines and custom endpoints for sending notifications out to external systems (support.kayako.com articles 1170 and 1146). Docked a point because the documentation estate is split across developer.kayako.com, support.kayako.com, help.kayako.com, and classichelp.kayako.com, and it is often unclear which applies to the current cloud product versus Kayako Classic.

pricing.model: Pay-per-resolution: billed only when the Kay AI agent fully resolves a ticket without human escalation. Kayako advertises no seat fees and no setup fees, though third-party trackers report an undisclosed base subscription alongside it.

plans.name: Kay AI Agent
plans.notes: Charged only when Kay fully resolves an issue without human escalation. Kayako states escalations and partial resolutions are not billed. No seat fees, no setup fees per kayako.com/pricing.

plans.name: Kayako One (full platform)
plans.price: Not published on kayako.com; third-party trackers report ~$79/month
plans.notes: Unified inbox, ticketing system, knowledge base, live chat widget, automation rules, reporting and analytics, plus Kay at $1/resolution and white-glove onboarding. Kayako's own pricing page does not state a base price for this bundle — the ~$79 figure comes from third-party pricing trackers and could not be confirmed against a primary source.

pricingBreakdown: Kayako's pricing page makes a genuinely appealing promise — no seats, no setup fee, $1 only when the AI actually closes a ticket — and then declines to publish anything you could build a budget from. That combination is the problem. Independent pricing trackers keep reporting a Kayako One base around $79/month that the official page never mentions, and I could not confirm or refute it from a primary source; Kayako publishes no plan table, no contract minimum, and no billing terms, and routes you to sales instead. So before comparing anything, understand that you are comparing against a number you have not been told. On the part that is published: $1 per resolution is the most expensive per-resolution rate of any AI agent reviewed on this site. Intercom's Fin is $0.99 and Help Scout's AI Answers is $0.75, and all three use the same billing trigger — a session closed without human escalation. Intercom in particular sells Fin standalone at $0.99/resolution with no seats required, bolted onto a helpdesk you already run, which is precisely Kayako's pitch at a lower unit price from a vendor with a far larger public evidence base. Where Kayako's math genuinely wins is against seat-based incumbents at low headcount and high repetitive volume: a 3-person team fielding 500 password-reset-grade tickets a month pays $500 in resolutions where Zendesk Suite Professional alone would cost $345 in seats before a single AI fee. Where it stops working is the mirror image — high-touch tickets that Kay escalates are free, which sounds great until you realise you are then paying for a helpdesk whose seat price you were never quoted.

capabilities.note: This is the entire product thesis now, and the most credible part of it. Kay is agentic rather than conversational-only — Kayako documents it creating users, issuing refunds, updating records, and closing cases, which is a meaningfully higher bar than drafting a reply for a human to send. Recent Capterra reviewers back this up specifically rather than generically: one April 2026 admin said Kay handles the top of the funnel cleanly enough that his team barely touches password resets. What you cannot verify is how well it holds up outside tidy repetitive queues, because the published accuracy numbers come from the vendor and its own sister companies.

Semantic search on the help center feeds Kay's answers, which is the standard modern pattern — your documentation quality is directly upstream of your AI quality here. The genuinely clever bit is the loop running the other way: when a ticket escalates to a human, Kayako drafts a knowledge base article from the resolution and asks a human to approve or edit it before publishing. That is a real answer to why knowledge bases rot, and it is not something Zendesk or Help Scout do as cleanly.

The twenty-year-old core underneath the AI story, and it is competent rather than exciting. Reviewers consistently describe the ticket interface as lightweight and fast to work in, with ticket notes singled out as a strength. The recurring specific gripe is the absence of native auto-refresh, which is a small thing that becomes an irritating thing in a busy queue. Channel breadth is narrower than Zendesk's — no evidence of native WhatsApp, Instagram DM, or SMS.

The weakest documented area, and unusually consistent across sources. A Capterra reviewer put it in three words — 'Analytics is the weak spot' — and independent review roundups describe reports buried under menus that are not laid out intuitively. If you need CSAT trending, deflection-rate reporting, and agent performance dashboards you can actually navigate, treat this as a demo blocker rather than something to sort out after signing.

Better than the marketing page alone suggests. There is a real developer portal at developer.kayako.com with a REST API, documented incoming webhooks for pushing external events onto customer timelines, custom endpoints for outbound notifications, and an official Zapier app with its own setup guide. Macros are properly documented too, and do more than canned text — eight distinct actions in one click. The caveat is archaeological: the docs are scattered across four domains (developer, support, help, and classichelp), and it is frequently unclear whether an article describes the current cloud product or Kayako Classic. Verify that anything you rely on applies to what you are actually buying.

pros: Genuinely agentic AI — Kay takes actions (refunds, user creation, record updates, ticket closure) rather than only drafting text for a human to approve
Outcome-aligned billing: you pay only when a ticket is fully resolved without human escalation, with escalations and partial resolutions explicitly not charged
The auto-drafted knowledge base article on every human escalation is a smart, underrated answer to knowledge-base rot
Lightweight, fast ticket interface with well-liked internal notes — 176 Capterra reviews averaging 4.0/5 reflect a mature, working core product
Long operating history (since 2001) and an enterprise security posture — SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, SSO/SAML — that many AI-first startups in this category cannot match
cons: Pricing is advertised as transparent but is not: no plan table, no billing terms, no contract minimums, and third-party trackers report a ~$79/month base that Kayako's own pricing page never mentions

At $1 per resolution it is the priciest per-resolution AI on this site — above Intercom's Fin ($0.99) and Help Scout's AI Answers ($0.75) — while offering a far thinner public evidence base than either
Analytics and reporting are the consistently weakest area, called out by name in recent reviews and independent roundups alike
The headline 68% resolution claim is unaudited, and the flagship case studies (Trilogy, Aurea) are ESW Capital sister companies rather than independent customers

Billing disputes are the dominant theme in negative Trustpilot reviews — erroneous invoices after documented cancellation, and an unexpected multi-year invoice — which is an uncomfortable pairing with pricing this opaque

The post-pivot evidence base is thin: Trustpilot carries only 22 reviews total, and the glowing AI-specific ones cluster tightly in April-May 2026, so there is very little independent long-run data on how Kay performs
Product future is not publicly committed: no roadmap, changelog, or release notes, under an owner whose model is buying mature software and running it lean

Documentation is fragmented across four domains (developer, support, help, classichelp) with the legacy Kayako Classic — in maintenance mode with no new features — still muddying search results for the current product
Voice is listed as a channel but disputed by a recent reviewer, and there is no evidence of native WhatsApp, Instagram DM, or SMS support

bestFor: Small-to-mid support teams with a genuinely repetitive ticket mix (password resets, order status, account changes) where a 50-70% deflection rate is plausible
Teams with low agent headcount but high ticket volume, where per-resolution billing beats multiplying a seat price
Buyers who want an AI agent that can actually execute actions in Stripe and Shopify, not just answer questions about them
Organisations replacing an aging legacy helpdesk who value SOC 2 Type II and SSO/SAML over channel breadth
verdict: I want to like the bet Kayako is making. Pay only when the AI actually closes the ticket is the most honest unit of value anyone in this category has landed on, and Kay is genuinely agentic — it issues refunds and updates records rather than drafting text for a human to rubber-stamp. The knowledge base article it auto-drafts on every escalation is the kind of detail that only comes from someone who has watched a knowledge base rot in production. But I cannot get past how much of this is unverifiable. Kayako calls its pricing transparent on a page with no plan table, no billing terms and no contract minimum, while independent trackers report a ~$79/month base the page never acknowledges — I could not confirm that figure from any primary source, so assume you are negotiating blind. The 68% resolution rate is unaudited, and the case studies proving it are Trilogy and Aurea, sister companies under the same ESW Capital ownership: that is marketing with extra steps, not evidence. Worse, billing complaints dominate the negative reviews — erroneous invoices after a documented cancellation, a surprise multi-year invoice — precisely the failure mode you do not want from a vendor that won't publish prices. Trustpilot has 22 reviews total, the glowing AI ones clustered into a six-week window right after the relaunch. That is a lot of trust to extend for the priciest per-resolution rate on this site, when Intercom sells standalone Fin at $0.99 with no seats and a far deeper public record. Demo it, and get every number in writing.
